data.name: Croatia
data.summary: Croatia taxes dividends at a flat 12%. Gains on securities are taxed at 12% only if they are sold within 2 years, and are untaxed after that. Real estate gains are 24% within 2 years. Children are exempt from inheritance and gift tax, and there is no wealth tax. No special regime for wealthy arrivals.

regimes.name: Ordinary tax residence
regimes.description: Worldwide taxation of residents; capital income taxed at a flat 12% final rate.
regimes.eligibility: Tax resident through a home in Croatia available for 183+ days or 183+ days' presence (PwC).

capital_gains.summary: Gains on financial assets (shares, bonds, fund units, business shares) are taxed at 12% only if sold within 2 years of acquisition; after 2 years they are not taxed (Art. 67 Income Tax Act). Real estate gains are taxed at 24% if sold within 2 years, otherwise exempt (Art. 58).
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Financial assets held 2+ years: not taxed. Transfers between spouses and close relatives, on divorce or inheritance: not taxed. Real estate: exempt after 2 years or if used as the seller's or close family's home.
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: FIFO record keeping; losses offset only gains of the same year. Real estate: selling more than three properties of the same type within five years is taxable regardless of holding period.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Gifted assets sold within 2 years of the donor's acquisition are taxed using the donor's acquisition date. Gains on shares not tradable on a capital market are assessed by the Tax Administration (12%). Share grants/options: 24%.

capital_gains.rate_basis: Rates assume holding beyond 2 years (0%). Within 2 years: 12% on financial assets, 24% on real estate (24% is the headline). No municipal surtax applies.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Trading as a registered business activity is taxed as self-employment income at progressive local rates (up to 33% in Zagreb, 2025) rather than capital income; frequent real estate dealing (more than three same-type properties in five years) is taxed at 24%.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: Financial assets and real estate: taxable only if disposed of within 2 years of acquisition.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Residents taxed on worldwide gains under the same rules; foreign tax credited per item on proof from the foreign authority (Art. 80).

dividends.summary: Dividends and profit shares are taxed at a flat 12% final tax (Art. 70 Income Tax Act), domestic or foreign. Foreign withholding tax is credited.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: No allowance. Certain exemptions (dividends reinvested into share capital) exist.

dividends.rate_basis: Flat 12% on gross dividends; withheld at source for Croatian dividends; foreign dividends self-assessed with a per-item foreign tax credit (Art. 80). A 15% US/EU WHT may exceed the 12% Croatian tax, leaving no Croatian tax and an excess credit that is not refunded.
dividends.withholding_outbound: 10% WHT on dividends to non-resident companies (0% to qualifying EU/EEA/Swiss parents with 10%/2-year holding); treaty rates 0–15% (PwC).
dividends.treaty_network: About 70 treaties listed by PwC. No US treaty in force found (one was signed in 2022; status not verified).

wealth_tax.summary: Croatia has no net wealth tax and no levy on financial assets.

wealth_tax.property_tax_note: Since 1 Jan 2025 municipalities must levy a property tax of EUR 0.60–8.00 per m² on residential property not used for permanent living or let long-term (replaced the holiday-home tax). A family's main home is outside its scope.

inheritance.summary: Inheritance and gift tax is 4% on cash, receivables, securities and movables (Local Taxes Act), but spouses and direct-line descendants and ancestors are exempt for both gifts and inheritances. Real estate passing to children is exempt from the 3% real estate transfer tax.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: Direct line (children, grandchildren, parents), spouse and adopted children exempt from the 4% tax. Real estate transfer tax exemption covers direct-line descendants and ancestors only (not spouses, per the Tax Administration page).
inheritance.important_exceptions: Siblings and in-laws are exempt only if they lived in the same household. Others pay 4% (movables only above EUR 6,700 each) and 3% RETT on real estate.

open_questions: The exempt-relative list rests on Tax Administration guidance; the article of the Local Taxes Act was not read directly.
inheritance.spouse_note: Spouses (including out-of-wedlock and life partners) are exempt from the 4% inheritance and gift tax on cash, securities and movables (Local Taxes Act); the Tax Administration says the 3% real estate transfer tax exemption covers direct-line relatives only, so Croatian real estate could still bear 3%.
inheritance.gift_tax: Same 4% tax applies to gifts; gifts to children are exempt. Gifts of shares to children are also not a capital-gains disposal (Art. 67).
inheritance.foreign_assets: The tax applies to property received in Croatia; children are exempt in any case.

regimes.name: Family holding company (d.o.o.)
regimes.description: The family holds the portfolio through a Croatian d.o.o. owned by the parents. Dividends received from companies are not taxed in the company (Art. 6(1) item 1 Profit Tax Act), with no minimum holding. Realised gains on shares are part of its profit and bear profit tax at 18% (10% only if the company's revenue is below EUR 1m a year). Money taken out as dividends is taxed again at 12%. Wealth tax (none) and inheritance tax (direct line exempt) are the same as for direct holding, so those metrics are inherited from the standard regime. For a Croatian resident, personal holding is the lower-tax route (gains on financial assets are untaxed after 2 years and dividends bear 12%); the company is shown because advisers use it to defer the 12% on dividends.
regimes.eligibility: Any Croatian resident can found a d.o.o. (share capital and formalities not researched). Contributing an existing portfolio in kind is a disposal for the individual, untaxed when the financial assets were held over 2 years (Art. 67 Income Tax Act); the company's cost basis was not researched.
regimes.duration_note: A corporate structure under ordinary law with no time limit; it lasts as long as the company exists.

structure.entity: drustvo s ogranicenom odgovornoscu (d.o.o.), a private limited company holding securities
structure.payout_notes: Dividends and profit shares paid to a resident individual are taxed by withholding at 12% (Art. 70 para. 19 Income Tax Act; Tax Administration: final tax at 12%), with no municipal surtax. Loans to shareholders, salaries and private use of company assets were not researched.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: Dividend relief (Art. 6(1) item 1 Profit Tax Act): the payer must be subject to profit tax or a similar tax, be a legal form comparable to a capital company, and the payment must not have been deductible for the payer; no percentage or holding period is stated in the article. Dividends from investment funds or ETFs (not capital companies) were not researched. Revenue of EUR 1m or more a year puts the company at 18% instead of 10% (Art. 28). General anti-avoidance and CFC rules were not researched.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: Not researched: tax on liquidation proceeds and on the sale of the d.o.o. shares by the family (gains on shares of a company not tradable on a capital market are taxed at 12%, Art. 70 para. 17 Income Tax Act).

dividends.exemptions_thresholds: No minimum holding or percentage stated in Art. 6(1) item 1; the payer must be subject to profit tax, comparable in legal form to a capital company, and not have deducted the payment.

income.name: Croatia

income_tax.summary: Cities set their own income tax rates. Zagreb applies 23% up to EUR 60,000 of annual taxable income and 33% above (decision NN 28/2025, in force from 1 March 2025; no 2026 change found). The basic personal allowance is EUR 600 a month (EUR 7,200 a year). Employees pay 20% pension contributions (15% + 5%) up to EUR 143,496 a year; employer pays health insurance.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: UNVERIFIED: 36.5% is the pension (15% first pillar + 5% second pillar) plus health insurance (16.5%) rates as generally stated for the self-employed; no opened page gives the self-employed rates or contribution base. The Tax Administration craftsman page (porezna-uprava.gov.hr) only confirms that craftspeople owe mandatory contributions and shows no rates; PwC's Croatian other-taxes page covers employees only (employee 20%: 15% + 5%, cap EUR 143,496 a year for first-pillar payments; the 16.5% health rate there is an employer contribution). The contribution base for the self-employed (fixed minimum vs actual income) is not established, so 36.5% on all income without a cap may overstate. Sole traders with receipts up to EUR 60,000 and no VAT registration can pay a lump-sum tax assessed by the tax administration (amounts not given).
income_tax.local_tax_note: Zagreb has no surtax; each city sets lower and higher rates itself (permitted ranges 15% to 23% and 25% to 33%; Zagreb uses the maximum 23% and 33%). Smaller towns and municipalities can charge less.

regimes.name: Digital nomad temporary stay
regimes.description: Temporary stay for digital nomads: a non-EU national employed by, or working through communication technology for, a company (or own company) not registered in Croatia and not serving employers in Croatia (Zakon o strancima art. 3 definition, art. 57 point 11), valid up to 18 months and extendable once within that period (art. 61), with a six-month wait before a new application (art. 57(4)). Remote Work Europe gives the income test as 2.5 times the average net monthly wage (EUR 3,622.50 a month in 2026, EUR 43,470 a year, or savings of the same amount); the Ordinance (Pravilnik) with the amount was not opened. Tax: Income Tax Act art. 9(1) point 26 says income tax is not paid on 'receipts of natural persons earned from dependent work or activity for an employer not registered in the Republic of Croatia on the basis of acquired digital nomad status under a special regulation'. This is a statutory exemption of the holder's remote-work pay regardless of where it is performed, so it covers work done while living in Croatia (covers_local_work true). The statute speaks of an 'employer'; whether freelance fees from foreign clients count equally is assumed from the definition of a digital nomad (own company or services for non-Croatian firms), not tested. Remote Work Europe adds that holders are treated as non-residents for tax beyond 183 days; not verified from the statute.
regimes.duration_note: Up to 18 months, no renewal; six-month cooling-off period.

succession.name: Croatia
succession.summary: Children, a spouse and partners are guaranteed half of their intestate share, and dependent parents a third. A foreign resident can choose the law of their nationality (EU Succession Regulation art. 22). Croatia has no trusts, and foundations are for public benefit only.
succession.reserved_share: Descendants, adopted children, spouse and registered or informal partners: half of their intestate share. Parents and other ancestors: one third of the intestate share, only if permanently unable to work and without means (Succession Act, Zakon o nasljeđivanju). A forced heir can be excluded only on grounds the will states.
succession.foreign_law_note: EU Succession Regulation: the law of the last habitual residence applies by default (art. 21), but a resident foreign national may choose the law of their nationality (art. 22).
succession.trust_note: Croatia is not in the HCCH table for the 1985 Trusts Convention. Croatian law has no trust. Foundations (zaklade) are governed by the Foundations Act, NN 106/18, 98/19, 151/22, and serve a public-benefit or charitable purpose.
open_questions: Succession Act article numbers not captured (e-Justice cites none).
Foundation purposes taken from search snippets, not the statute text.

assumptions: Positions are held for more than two years, as the tax file assumes, so gains on financial assets are untaxed personally. A family that sells within two years pays 12%.
The company check uses the 18% rate (revenue of EUR 1m or more a year), as the real family's income is far above that; the 10% rate for revenue below EUR 1m is left out.
Foreign dividends carry 15% withholding, above the 12% Croatian rate, so foreign dividends bear no Croatian tax personally.
No allowances apply to capital income.
open_questions: Foundation and trust were considered and not added: no family-wealth foundation or trust in common use was found (not researched against a statute).

Whether exempt dividends count as revenue for the EUR 1m threshold of Art. 28 was not confirmed; accounting revenue is assumed. If they do not, the company check's 18% could be 10% for a smaller portfolio.

The Profit Tax Act was read in part (Art. 6, 7, 28, 30); Art. 80 para. 1 (the cap of the foreign tax credit at the Croatian tax) was not seen in the extract, so the credit cap in the personal checks rests on the item-by-item rule (para. 2) and on the Tax Administration practice.
The Local Taxes Act article for the inheritance exemption was not read; the exemption rests on the Tax Administration pages.

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally
paths.note: Dividends bear a 12% final tax (Art. 70 Income Tax Act); foreign tax is credited per item, so a 15% foreign withholding leaves no Croatian tax on foreign dividends. Gains on financial assets sold after 2 years are untaxed (Art. 67 para. 8). Direct-line heirs and the spouse are exempt from inheritance tax; there is no wealth tax.

paths.name: Family holding d.o.o.
paths.note: A Croatian d.o.o. owned by the parents holds the portfolio. Dividends it receives are deducted from its base (Art. 6(1) item 1 Profit Tax Act); realised gains bear profit tax at 18% (10% below EUR 1m revenue). Payouts bear 12%. The parents' estate holds the d.o.o. shares; direct-line heirs are exempt. Worse than personal holding: gains untaxed after 2 years personally, but taxed at 18% inside the company.
